planting.note: Plant dormant tubers 2-3 inches deep in fall into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath deciduous trees where spring light reaches the ground before leaf-out.

directions: Named for a German alpine plantsman who selected it among seed-grown solida populations, this cultivar bears unusually large, dusky salmon-pink flowers packed into dense upright spikes above finely cut, grey-green foliage. Like other spring corydalis it is a true ephemeral, racing from emergence through bloom and seed-set in a matter of weeks before disappearing underground for the remainder of the year. Tuck the dormant tubers among later-emerging ferns and hostas so nothing marks the bare ground once the clump vanishes in early summer. Established colonies thicken steadily from self-sown seed and offset tubers, naturalizing under deciduous canopy over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring into gritty, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, mimicking the limestone cliff crevices this species roots into in the wild.

directions: Native to limestone cliff faces in southern China, this fibrous-rooted species forms a tidy, semi-evergreen rosette of ferny, blue-green leaves that persists far longer into the season than the spring-ephemeral tuberous corydalis. From spring into fall it sends up a steady, extended succession of tubular, golden-yellow flowers rather than a single concentrated bloom flush, making it a useful long-season filler for the shade border. Because it roots naturally into narrow rock crevices, it strongly prefers sharply drained, gritty soil and resents sitting wet, especially over winter. Site it in dappled shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun to keep the foliage from scorching.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool spring weather into consistently moist, humus-rich soil under high shade; avoid letting the fibrous roots dry out during establishment.

directions: A Himalayan and west Chinese woodlander related to the popular flexuosa-group blues, this species carries finely divided, grey-green ferny foliage and clusters of gently curved, spurred flowers in clear blue to violet-blue tones through late spring and into summer. Unlike the tuberous spring-ephemeral corydalis, its fibrous root system keeps the clump present and semi-evergreen for a longer stretch of the growing season before it eases into dormancy. It is unforgiving of drought even briefly during active growth, so a steady, cool, consistently moist root run is essential to keeping the planting vigorous year over year. Give it high, dappled shade and rich woodland soil, dividing congested clumps in earliest spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring into lean, sharply drained soil; this species tolerates drier conditions than most corydalis once its woody base is established.

directions: Collected in China and named for the plant hunter who introduced many East Asian woodland species to Western gardens, this subshrubby corydalis builds a persistent, slightly woody base topped with finely cut, glaucous blue-gray foliage that holds its color through the heat of summer. Clear yellow, spurred flowers appear over a long stretch from spring into summer rather than in one brief flush, giving it more sustained garden presence than the spring-ephemeral tuberous species. Its woody crown and lean-soil preference make it noticeably more drought- and heat-tolerant than typical woodland corydalis, a useful trait in warmer gardens. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil with a few hours of dappled sun and avoid rich, consistently wet conditions that encourage rot.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil in dappled shade; established clumps tolerate somewhat warmer, drier summers than most blue-flowered corydalis.

directions: Often grown as a more garden-tolerant stand-in for the celebrated but temperamental flexuosa-group blues, this Chinese woodland species produces the same finely cut, ferny foliage and clear sky-blue, tubular flowers through spring into early summer. Its fibrous root system reportedly shrugs off warm, humid summers better than its more famous relatives, making it a worthwhile option for gardeners south of the cool-summer belt where flexuosa selections struggle. Flowering is prolonged under cool spring conditions and tapers as temperatures rise, with the clump easing into a lighter summer presence rather than vanishing completely. Provide dappled shade, steady moisture, and humus-rich soil, dividing congested clumps in earliest spring to increase the planting.
